history.heading: Maya and Pipil
paragraphs: El Salvador, the smallest country in Central America, was inhabited by Maya peoples and later by the Pipil, a Nahua people who called their land Cuscatlán. Joya de Cerén, a Maya farming village buried by volcanic ash around 600 CE and preserved like a "Pompeii of the Americas", is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Spanish conquistadors led by Pedro de Alvarado invaded in 1524 and met strong resistance before establishing control.

history.heading: Independence and coffee oligarchy
paragraphs: El Salvador gained independence from Spain in 1821, was part of the Federal Republic of Central America and became fully independent in 1841. In the late 19th century coffee became the main export, and land was concentrated in the hands of a small elite, often called the "fourteen families".

In 1932 a peasant uprising was crushed by the military in La Matanza ("the massacre"), in which thousands of mostly indigenous people were killed. Military governments ruled for most of the following decades.

history.heading: Civil war and after
paragraphs: A civil war from 1979 to 1992 pitted the US-backed military government against the leftist FMLN guerrillas. About 75,000 people were killed, including Archbishop Óscar Romero, assassinated in 1980 and later canonised. The 1992 peace accords ended the war.

After the war, gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which originated among Salvadoran migrants in Los Angeles, spread violence, making El Salvador one of the world's most dangerous countries. Nayib Bukele, elected in 2019, launched a crackdown from 2022 under a state of emergency, with mass arrests, which sharply reduced homicides.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Spanish is the official language, and the Nahuat language is being revived. Most Salvadorans are Catholic, with a large evangelical population. Pupusas, thick corn tortillas stuffed with cheese, beans or pork, are the national dish.
A large Salvadoran diaspora lives in the United States. Football is the most popular sport, and surfing at beaches such as El Tunco attracts visitors.

politics.heading: Concentration of power
paragraphs: El Salvador is a presidential republic. President Bukele was re-elected in 2024 despite a constitutional ban on consecutive terms, after a court ruling allowed it, and his party controls the Legislative Assembly. In 2025 the constitution was changed to allow indefinite re-election.

His security policies are very popular domestically, but human rights groups criticise mass detentions without due process and the weakening of checks and balances. El Salvador agreed to hold deportees from the United States in its mega-prison, CECOT.

economy.heading: Remittances and Bitcoin
paragraphs: El Salvador's economy relies heavily on remittances from Salvadorans in the US, which make up around a quarter of GDP, as well as on services, textile assembly (maquilas) and agriculture such as coffee and sugar.

The country has used the US dollar since 2001. In 2021 it became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender, though acceptance was made voluntary in 2025 under an IMF agreement. Improved security has boosted tourism.
